ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was provided by the ethics committee of the Faculty of Psychology, Ruhr University Bochum (approval number: 650).
All participants provided written informed consent.
Participants were asked to rate depressive symptoms over the past day (i.e. previous 24 hours), with the weight gain/loss item removed (as implemented by Holmes et al., 2016).
table.formatted: Participants were asked to rate depressive symptoms over the past day (i.e. previous 24 hours), with the weight gain/loss item removed (as implemented by <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Holmes et al., 2016)</ref>.

table.text: Participants completed the daily QIDS each day over the entire course of the study.
To cross-validate the daily QIDS as a measure of treatment success, participants completed the standard version of the QIDS (asking about the past seven days) at each research assessment.
At the initial eligibility assessment participants provided written informed consent and were then assisted to register on the online study platform.
After finishing the questionnaires, participants were introduced to the baseline phase ('A') of the study, completing the daily QIDS each day for two weeks.
During the baseline phase participants completed the daily QIDS each day.

At the end of the baseline participants had another appointment with the researcher during which they completed questionnaires including the QIDS and were then randomized to complete either the imagery CBM or CCT intervention first (see supplements for details of randomization procedures).

During the first intervention phase participants were scheduled to complete 8 sessions of their allocated first intervention (imagery CBM or CCT) from home on their computer or other compatible device.
At the end of the first intervention phase participants had another appointment with the researcher during which they completed questionnaires including the QIDS.
At the final assessment participants completed a last set of questionnaires including the QIDS, after which they were debriefed about the study.
Participants were 3 men and 4 women, with mean age of 46.86 (SD = 17.62, range 24 -69).

Higher BFs indicate more support for the null hypothesis relative to the alternative hypothesis (i.e. indicate lack of improvement relative to previous phase) After the first five participants had completed the study, results from an RCT that had started in parallel (Blackwell et al., 2023) became available and suggested some improvements that could be made to the intervention.

table.text: For each hedonic domain participants were asked to list two of their favourite activities or experiences.
Participants were randomized to one of either i) iCBM first or ii) CCT first, following completion of all baseline measures and discussion of the upcoming training schedule.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: For all except two participants a set of parameters could be found that would provide both a < 5% false-positive rate and > 80% power to find a greater rate of decrease in QIDS score in the intervention phase (see Table 4). For the two participants where this was not possible, in one case (participant 7) it was because they were already projected to reach a QIDS score of 0 by the end of the intervention phase. For the other, although it was possible to find a set of parameters, they provided only 72% power to find a feasible end QIDS score.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. text.text: Identifying whether a psychological intervention is providing the expected benefits for a patient is crucial if we wish to optimize treatment outcomes.

For example, noticing that a patient is not "on track" for a successful outcome provides the opportunity to intervene, for example via feedback to their therapist (e.g., de Jong et al., 2021; Lutz et al., 2022), or switching to another intervention.

text.text: Monitoring of treatment progress therefore plays a key role in personalization of psychological treatments (e.g., Deisenhofer et al., 2024; Nye et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Monitoring of treatment progress therefore plays a key role in personalization of psychological treatments (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Deisenhofer et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Nye et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Established methods for monitoring treatment progress largely rely on comparing the trajectory of repeated outcome measurements to benchmarks for expected trajectories, ideally based on large datasets (e.g., Lutz et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Established methods for monitoring treatment progress largely rely on comparing the trajectory of repeated outcome measurements to benchmarks for expected trajectories, ideally based on large datasets (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lutz et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, in the absence of suitable data, for example when interventions are novel or outcomes highly idiosyncratic, it would be helpful to be able to perform this monitoring at an individual patient level, that is, via a single case approach.
In a single case approach, the data provided by an individual patient is analysed without recourse to other external data.

Prior to starting a treatment the patient completes a baseline phase of repeated measurement only, and via comparison of the pattern of data in the treatment phase to the baseline phase, a judgement can be made as to whether the data are consistent with the treatment having an effect (e.g., Kazdin, 2011; Kininger et al., 2025; Morley, 2017).

text.text: With some exceptions (e.g., a changing criterion design), this judgement is normally made retrospectively, after treatment completion.
However, this is too late to affect the course of treatment itself, and ideally if a treatment is not working it would be useful to be able to identify this as soon as possible.

One method for analysing data as it accumulates that has received increasing attention in the context of between-group designs is sequential Bayesian analysis, for example based on calculation of Bayes factors, which provides a simple means for repeated analysis (even after PREPRINT v1.0 28.10.26 https://osf.io/qcwfx/ each new data point is collected) while preserving the statistical error rate at a desired level (Schönbrodt et al., 2017).

text.text: Within the context of randomized controlled trials, taking a sequential Bayesian approach can substantially reduce sample sizes by allowing ineffective treatments to be rapidly identified and discarded (Blackwell et al., 2019 (Blackwell et al., , 2023)).

text.text: Theoretically, applying this approach to single case data would mean that rather than relying on a fixed intervention period, data in the intervention phase would be analysed as it is obtained, and an ineffective treatment could be identified as soon as enough evidence had accumulated.
How might this work in practice?

The current paper introduces one potential method for applying sequential Bayesian analyses to single case data, building on the "leapfrog" randomized controlled trial approach outlined by Blackwell et al. (2019).

text.text: According to this approach, a patient would start with a baseline monitoring period during which they complete daily outcome measures.
Daily monitoring continues after initiation of treatment ('intervention period').

After a pre-specified minimum number of data points in the intervention period had been collected (Nmin), sequential Bayesian analysis would be initiated, comparing the data from the baseline phase to the data collected so far in the intervention phase.

Specifically, a Bayes factor would be calculated that quantified the relative likelihood of the observed data under the null hypothesis (no improvement in the intervention phase compared to the baseline phase) relative to the alternative hypothesis (that there is improvement in the intervention phase compared to the baseline phase).

If at any point a pre-specified Bayes factor threshold for failure (BFfail) were reached, providing sufficient evidence for the null hypothesis, the treatment could be discontinued and a different treatment could be tried, or some kind of modification or augmentation could be attempted .

A time limit (Nmax days/data points) would be set for the treatment to demonstrate efficacy; if the Bayes factor had not yet reached a pre-specified threshold for success (BFsuccess) by this point, then it would also be concluded that the treatment was not sufficiently effective.

The exact specification of these parameters (Nmin, PREPRINT v1.0 28.10.26 https://osf.io/qcwfx/ Nmax, BFfail, BFsuccess; see Table 1 for an overview) would determine the sensitivity to detect whether an intervention is effective or not, as well as the efficiency of the design.

text.text: Applying such an approach to single case data could theoretically bring further advantages: using the baseline phase data to simulate possible continuations into the intervention phase would allow personalization of the parameters based on the individual's data and its characteristics.
For example, if the baseline data showed higher variability and higher levels of autocorrelation, it is likely that more intervention phase data would be needed to draw confident conclusions.

text.text: Possible continuations of the QIDS daily data were simulated over a range of possible treatment effects.
A first order autoregressive model was fitted to the baseline data, and then continuations were simulated with the same first order autoregressive structure.
A simple linear trend was fitted to the baseline data, and the variance around this trend line used as the variance in the simulated continuation.
That is, the continuations were personalized to the individual by taking the auto-regressive structure and variance from their baseline data.
The null model (i.e., no treatment effect) was then simulated as a continuation of the baseline data with the same linear trend.

Other possible continuations, reflecting different possible levels of treatment success, were defined in terms of the daily QIDS score reached at the end of a two-week intervention period, in intervals of two (e.g., if the null model resulted in a predicted QIDS score of 8 by the end of the two-week period, continuations with linear slopes leading to predicted QIDS scores of 6, 4, 2, and 0 were simulated).
A set of 1000 simulations were created for each possible QIDS end score.
Following simulation of each continuation, simulated QIDS scores were rounded to the nearest integer and predicted QIDS scores < 0 were changed to 0.

This study aimed to investigate the possibility of applying sequential Bayesian The study demonstrated a simulation-based method for generating a set of decision parameters and by applying this retrospectively to the collected data found that in 5 cases the first intervention would have been stopped earlier than the two-week trial period, and that in one case it would have identified the treatment as effective.
The study demonstrated that in principle the approach could be applied and could bring some of the hypothesised advantages.

That is, personalized decision parameters could be derived based on each patient's individual data pattern in the baseline (e.g., including the variability, autocorrelation, and slope), and potentially this could lead to shortened decision times in the presence of an ineffective intervention.
However, the study also illustrated potential complexities of taking a simulation-based approach to trial planning.

Specifically, although simulating the null hypothesis, i.e., continuation of the trajectory from the baseline phase, is relatively straightforward, simulating successful treatment outcomes requires more complex decision-making, which in turn will affect the power of the design to detect PREPRINT v1.0 28.10.26 https://osf.io/qcwfx/ successful or unsuccessful treatments.

text.text: While the current study chose one way of defining and simulating successful outcomes for demonstration purposes, there are of course many different ways one could do this.

It could also be argued that in the case of the "failures", simple visual analysis would lead one to conclude that the treatments were not effective much faster than the Bayesian analyses, which seemed relatively inefficient in practice.
This could reflect the analysis method being relatively conservative within the context of the measurement schedule used in the current study.

This study applied a particular kind of analysis in a specific intervention context, but there would be many different ways to apply the basic idea, that is, using a participant's own baseline data to simulate a range of possible continuations and using these to determine a set of appropriate analysis and decision parameters with the desired statistical power and falsepositive rate.

For example, while this study took the de Vries and Morey (2013) method for Bayesian single case analyses as a ready-to-use "off the shelf" R package (Morey & de Vries, 2014), there are other ways in which Bayesian analyses could be applied, and the general principles could also be applied to non-Bayesian analyses.

text.text: Consideration of the method used in the current study and the results obtained does raise a number of factors that researchers or clinicians would need to think through in applying this or similar methods.
First, the question of the appropriate measure for the analyses and the frequency of measurement and analysis is key for determining the utility of the approach.

In the current study an adapted daily measure of the ultimate clinical outcome, PREPRINT v1.0 28.10.26 https://osf.io/qcwfx/ symptoms of depression, was used, with the rationale that changes in these symptoms would be the crucial criterion for determining whether the treatment had worked.

text.text: However, this is a relatively "blunt" measure and potentially a more sensitive and specific measure focussing on e.g., a mechanism targeted by the intervention could have been more appropriate; such a measure might not only be more sensitive to detecting intervention success, reducing the potential false-negative error rate, but also make it easier to detect treatment failure earlier on, in that a lack of early change would provide a clear signal of no effect.

The daily measurement schedule was chosen based on previous literature using the interventions, which indicated that for one of the interventions (the imagery CBM), observable change should happen within one week (e.g., Blackwell & Holmes, 2010; Lang et al., 2012).

text.text: However, with other interventions where the timescale of change is expected to be slower it might be that such frequent data collection does not add additional useful information, and that daily repeated analyses are not appropriate.
Therefore, the exact measurement and analysis schedule would need to be adjusted to the treatment applied.
Practical considerations could also play a role in these decisions.

For example, in the case of remotely-delivered interventions that are not tied to a particular appointment schedule, daily testing and decision-making could be helpful in switching someone to a new intervention as soon as treatment failure is detected.

Conversely, when a treatment is tied to weekly appointments, it could be questioned whether finding out that a treatment is not working after 5 days offers any real advantage to finding out at the appointment 2 days later, except in the case of acute risk, and hence repeated analyses could simply be tied to appointment dates.
Another question in the context of an open-ended intervention is what to do with the knowledge that an intervention has hit the success criterion, BFsuccess.
In this case one would continue with the intervention, but potentially it would be then useful to build in a mechanism to detect if it ceases to bring further benefits.

Finally, while some patients may PREPRINT v1.0 28.10.26 https://osf.io/qcwfx/ welcome rapid detection of a lack of treatment effect and having the chance to try something else, others may interpret this as a sign of personal failure or treatment-resistance, or nevertheless wish to continue with the ineffective treatment.

text.text: Use of this sequential approach and any treatment-switching decisions would therefore need to be carefully discussed, explained, and agreed with each individual patient.

While the purpose of this study was to illustrate the basic principles of the approach, it applied the sequential analyses and determined the personalized sets of analysis parameters retrospectively, which could introduce some bias into the decision parameters chosen.
This retrospective nature also means that it could not demonstrate "live" application of the decision-making and how that would work from a practical perspective.
The study also applied the ideas in a somewhat artificial approach with fixed baseline and intervention timeperiods.
For this reason, the simulations relating to determining the decision parameters were only applied to the transition from the baseline to the first intervention.
However, in a "realworld" application it might also be worth using the baseline data to make decisions on how to proceed with the next intervention phase.

For example, if a participant's data were showing high variability and autocorrelation in the baseline it might be useful to extend the baseline further to acquire more data points, or if a participant's baseline data were already showing a strong downward trend (as was the case for several participants in this study, see Figure 1), it may also not make sense to introduce an intervention, first because it may not be necessary at that time, and second because it would be infeasible to detect treatment success.

text.text: Overall, this study presents the idea of applying sequential Bayesian analyses to single case data and illustrates one method for doing this, applied retrospectively to data collected from outpatients completing computerized interventions.
While demonstrating the basic idea, the study raises a number of questions about potential future implementations and it seems likely that further optimization will be useful.
However, in principle, building on this basic idea opens a number of opportunities, perhaps especially in relation to remotely-delivered https://osf.io/qcwfx/ (e.g., web-or app-based) interventions.

text.text: These were then implemented for the final two participants.
Specifically, the initial instructions for each session were adjusted so that they were a little more varied from session to session and included a 'tip of the day' that was different each time.
Further, at the end of each session there were instructions and suggestions to practice recalling and rehearsing the training scenarios in daily life (e.g., when encountering similar situation).

This was then reinforced by asking participants at the start of each session to rate i) how often they deliberately recalled training scenarios in between sessions; ii) how often in daily life they tried to imagine situations unfolding as if they were one of the training scenarios; iii) how often they experienced the training scenarios popping into their mind involuntarily since the last session.

The cognitive control training was an adaptive Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task (PASAT), as implemented in several studies investigating cognitive control training in the context of depression/rumination (e.g., Calkins et al., 2015; Hoorelbeke et al., 2015; Siegle et al., 2007).

text.text: The training aims to improve participants' control over the content of their cognitions, especially under conditions of stress, and thus increase their ability to disengage from maladaptive patterns of thinking such as rumination.

During the PASAT, participants heard a continuous stream of digits from 1 to 9 (presented via headphones), with the task of immediately calculating the sum of the last two digits heard and clicking a corresponding button (1-18).
Presentation of the digits was separated by an inter-stimulus interval (ISI) that started at 3000ms each session.
The ISI was then reduced by 100ms following four consecutive correct responses, or increased by 100ms following four consecutive incorrect responses.
In this way the difficulty of the task was adapted to the participant's performance and increased as their performance improved.
Participants received feedback on their performance via presentation of their ISI and number https://osf.io/qcwfx/ Dimensional Anhedonia Rating Scale (DARS; Rizvi et al., 2015).

text.text: The DARS is a 17-item self-report measure of different facets of anhedonia (desire, motivation, effort and consummatory pleasure) across different hedonic domains (hobbies/past-times, food/drinks, social activities, and sensory experiences).
For each hedonic domain participants were asked to list two of their favourite activities or experiences.
They then made ratings of the different facets of anhedonia on scales from 0 (not at all) to 4 (very much).

text.text: Training stimuli were audio recordings (~10 -15s) of mostly everyday scenarios, which were structured so that they started ambiguous but always resolved positively.
Participants were instructed to shut their eyes while listening to each scenario and imagine themselves in the situation described as if actively involved.

Via this repeated practice in imagining positive resolutions for ambiguous situations, the training aims to instil a bias to automatically imagine positive resolutions for ambiguous situations encountered in daily life.
The training schedule was adapted from that used by Westermann et al. (2021), using the training scenarios and general instructions from Blackwell et al. (2023).

text.text: The schedule started with an initial introductory session followed by 8 online sessions over two weeks (with four sessions scheduled for each week).
Sessions started with some brief mood ratings, followed by a reminder of the instructions and a practice scenario, and then 5 blocks of 8 scenarios (lasting about 15 -20 minutes).
After each scenario participants were asked to rate how vividly they had been able to imagine the scenario, on a scale from 1 (not at all vivid) to 7 (extremely vivid).

Between each block participants could take a brief break if needed, and were shown a graphical display of their vividness scores over the blocks completed so far, with instructions to reflect on these and try to improve or maintain their imagery vividness in the upcoming block.
Each session ended with brief ratings of state mood.
The introductory session included an extended introduction to mental imagery, with several practice examples, followed by 4 blocks of 5 scenarios.
